assignments.value: Overview produced using ChatGPT 5.2, extended thinking, combining SEP and Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, as well as Encyclopedia.com, using the following prompt:  Produce a framework outline for Rights Based Ethics based on the following websites:  •	https://www.encyclopedia.com/science/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/rights-theory  •	https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/united-states-and-canada/us-history/rights  •	https://iep.utm.edu/hum-rts/ https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/rights/  •	https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/rights-human/   The framework outline should follow the length and structure of the following https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/consequentialism/   Verify each reference in the original encyclopaedia articles and then give a list of all those references, insure that the references are listed accurately as they are presented in the original encyclopaedia articles.  Rights-Based Ethics (Rights Theory) — Extended Framework Outline  (entry-style structure modeled on the SEP “Consequentialism” format; ~3000 words excluding bibliography)  1.	Contents 2.	Introduction 3.	Genealogy and the Modern “Rights Turn” 4.	What a Right Is 5.	The Structure of Rights: Hohfeld and Correlatives 6.	Kinds of Rights and Their Practical Profiles 7.	Rights as Reasons: Trumps, Side-Constraints, and Conclusions 8.	What Grounds Rights? Competing Theories 9.	Human Rights as a Special Case 10.	Duties, Institutions, and Feasibility 11.	Conflicts, Limits, and the Problem of “Balancing” 12.	Application Domains: Science, Technology, and Biomedicine 13.	Objections and Persistent Problems 14.	Operational Procedure: A Repeatable “Rights-Based” Method 15.	Concluding Orientation  1. Introduction  Rights-based ethics is a family of moral approaches that treats rights as central in determining what may be done to individuals (and sometimes groups). Where outcome-focused moralities emphasize producing the best states of affairs, rights-based ethics emphasizes that certain persons have entitlements—freedoms, claims, protections, powers, immunities—that place constraints on how others may pursue goals, including socially beneficial goals. The basic thought is not merely that it is good when people enjoy freedoms and protections, but that others owe them these protections in ways that are not simply optional or easily overridden. The SEP entry captures the core concept succinctly: rights are entitlements—entitlements to do (or not do) certain actions, or to be (or not be) in certain states, and entitlements that others act (or refrain) toward us in certain ways.  As a “framework,” rights-based ethics can play two roles. First, it can be foundational: rights are treated as moral starting points that constrain permissible action. Second, it can be derivative: rights are conclusions generated by deeper moral commitments—such as equal standing, agency, welfare, or dignity—then used as “action-guides.” The Encyclopedia.com “Rights Theory” entry explicitly contrasts “rights as starting points” with “rights as conclusions,” and highlights the practical and justificatory tensions that come with each.  2. Genealogy and the Modern “Rights Turn” 2.1 From legal status to moral standing  Historically, “rights” language is deeply entangled with law—property, privilege, authority, and institutional standing. Modern philosophical debate, however, increasingly treats rights as moral notions that may criticize or justify law rather than merely recording it. The Encyclopedia.com “Rights” entry frames this as a key tension: even skeptics about “natural rights” typically concede the reality of legal rights, and jurisprudence has long tried to explain what those rights are and how they relate to duties.  2.2 The post-1945 global human-rights project  The contemporary “human rights” paradigm is shaped by international legal and moral practice and aims to protect people from severe abuses. The SEP “Human Rights” entry describes human rights as international norms protecting people everywhere from severe political, legal, and social abuses, and emphasizes that these rights exist in morality and law and are addressed primarily to governments. The IEP entry similarly presents human rights as moral guarantees tied to the conditions of a “minimally good life,” and notes how modern declarations and conventions (beginning centrally with the 1948 Universal Declaration) institutionalize this aspiration.  2.3 Why genealogy matters for a framework  Rights frameworks inherit two persistent legacies:  Institutional entanglement: rights claims often imply the need for courts, enforcement, and governance—so “having a right” is rarely just a private moral fact.  Justificatory pluralism: rights are defended by different moral theories (interest, will, equality, personhood, practice). As a result, a “rights-based ethics framework” must be explicit about which justifications it assumes when it assigns priority to rights.  3. What a Right Is  Rights-based ethics starts with a working definition: a right is an entitlement that structures what others may do and what they owe. The SEP entry emphasizes that rights can concern actions and states, and can impose constraints on others’ conduct toward the right-holder.  3.1 Moral vs legal rights  A crucial distinction is between legal rights and moral rights. Legal rights exist by virtue of enactment and institutional recognition. Moral rights purport to hold independently (or at least to justify what law should be). The IEP’s treatment of human rights repeatedly stresses that legal recognition strengthens efficacy, but the validity of human rights is characteristically taken not to be conditional upon recognition—i.e., moral rights can precede law.  3.2 Claim-rights and liberty-rights  Philosophers commonly distinguish claim-rights (others owe a duty) from liberty-rights (you have no duty not to do something; others lack a claim to stop you). The IEP’s conceptual analysis of human rights explicitly highlights this distinction as part of clarifying what a “right” is and how it functions.  This matters operationally: many disputes become clearer when we ask whether someone is asserting (a) a duty on others, or (b) a protected permission for themselves.  4. The Structure of Rights: Hohfeld and Correlatives  A recurring source of confusion in public debate is that “rights” is used as a single label for many different normative relations. Modern analysis often uses Hohfeld’s framework (as reflected in both encyclopedia discussions of rights theory and rights jurisprudence).  4.1 Hohfeldian “incidents”  Hohfeld-style analysis distinguishes at least four basic positions (each paired with a correlative):  •	Claim-right ↔ Duty •	Liberty (Privilege) ↔ No-claim •	Power ↔ Liability •	Immunity ↔ Disability  The point for a rights-based ethical framework is methodological: before arguing about priority, we should identify which normative relation is in play. The Encyclopedia.com “Rights” entry situates rights debates within jurisprudential attempts to explain such relations and their correlativity to duties.  4.2 Why correlativity matters  Rights typically imply directed obligations: if A has a claim-right, some duty-bearer(s) must have a duty. This pushes rights-based ethics toward institutional questions: who is the duty-bearer (state, corporation, professional, family member), and what is owed?  5. Kinds of Rights and Their Practical Profiles  Rights-based ethics must classify rights not only conceptually but also by how they operate socially.  5.1 Negative, positive, and the “mixed duties” point  A standard contrast labels rights as “negative” (non-interference) or “positive” (assistance/provision). But the Encyclopedia.com “Rights Theory” entry notes that even “freedom rights” can be expensive and institution-dependent (police, courts, “machinery of justice”), and suggests that the negative/positive distinction is often less helpful than focusing on basic rights and their real duty-structures. The Encyclopedia.com “Rights” entry (Wellman) develops this further through Shue’s view that every basic right imposes duties to forbear, protect, and aid, blending negative and positive requirements.  5.2 Welfare rights vs liberty rights  A central controversy concerns whether welfare claims (to health care, subsistence, social security) are genuine rights or only ideals. The “Rights” entry describes Cranston’s argument that universal welfare rights would impose impossible duties on poorer societies, and Nickel’s reply that civil and political rights also require costly institutions and that welfare rights may be realized progressively or in trimmed forms. A rights-based framework therefore needs an explicit view on feasibility: are rights strict requirements regardless of resources, or do they include progressive realization and “minimum core” content?  5.3 Who can be a right-holder? children, animals, groups  The “Rights” entry discusses debates about whether infants and non-human animals can hold rights, noting Feinberg’s attempt to combine will-theoretic elements (rights as claims) with interest-theoretic elements (representation of interests), and the subsequent dispute about whether animals have “interests” in the relevant sense. This matters because rights-based ethics often functions as a theory of moral standing: who counts as someone to whom duties are owed as a matter of right?  6. Rights as Reasons: Trumps, Side-Constraints, and Conclusions  Rights-based ethics is not only about listing rights; it is about how rights function in reasoning.  6.1 Rights as “trumps” (Dworkin)  The Encyclopedia.com “Rights Theory” entry highlights Dworkin’s view that rights can function as trumps against goal-based political decision-making (including utilitarian calculations), especially where majorities might impose burdens on minorities. It also emphasizes Dworkin’s foundational political morality: government must treat those it governs with equal concern and respect, and rights help prevent discrimination driven by “external preferences.” For a framework, this yields a rule of thumb: when a policy’s justification depends on counting preferences that deny equal status to some persons, rights-based reasoning treats those preferences as normatively suspect and often excluded.  6.2 Rights as “side-constraints” (Nozick-style)  The “Rights” entry also describes a rights conception where moral rights are side-constraints on pursuing goals: persons are inviolable and may not be used merely as means, so rights primarily impose negative duties not to injure, coerce, or interfere. This generates a distinctive decision procedure: we ask first whether an action violates constraints (coercion, theft, assault), not whether it improves outcomes.  6.3 Rights as conclusions (derivative rights)  The “Rights Theory” entry notes another route: rights are defended on broader grounds—including utilitarian ones—but then the language of rights becomes vulnerable to being “trumped” by competing goods unless the framework specifies why rights have special priority. So a mature rights framework must disclose whether it treats rights as:  lexically prior constraints,  high-weight considerations that can be overridden in rare cases, or  one value among others to be traded off.  7. What Grounds Rights? Competing Theories  A rights-based ethical framework needs a justification story—otherwise it risks degenerating into “rights assertion” without warrant.  7.1 Interest theory  On interest theories, rights protect sufficiently important interests (welfare, security, agency) such that others have duties. The IEP explicitly presents interest theory as one of the dominant approaches in philosophical justification of human rights and emphasizes its strengths and limitations. Interest theory fits well with rights for children, incapacitated persons, and (sometimes) animals, because it does not require the right-holder to exercise sophisticated choice.  7.2 Will theory  Will theories tie rights to normative control—choice, authority, powers to claim/waive. The IEP again presents will theory as the second dominant justification family and explores how it shapes the concept of a right. Will theory fits well with rights as protections of autonomy and self-determination, but can struggle with right-holders who cannot exercise choice.  7.3 Equality/personhood and hybrid accounts  The Encyclopedia.com “Rights Theory” entry emphasizes an equality-based grounding in Dworkin’s work (equal concern and respect) and the role of rights in blocking discriminatory majoritarianism. The “Rights” entry also gestures toward personhood/agency approaches (e.g., Griffin’s “personhood” framing and its link to autonomy, liberty, and welfare rights). In practice, many frameworks become pluralist: they borrow from interest, will, equality, and practice-based considerations to stabilize both moral appeal and institutional applicability.  8. Human Rights as a Special Case  Human rights are often treated as a subfamily of rights—distinct because of universality, political function, and institutionalization.  8.1 The “general idea” of human rights  The SEP “Human Rights” entry recommends clarifying the concept of human rights (not merely listing rights), identifying defining features and emphasizing that most human rights are claim-rights imposing duties that involve respect, protection, facilitation, and provision. The IEP similarly treats human rights as “public moral norms” aimed at securing the prerequisites for minimally good lives and as standards for morally auditing political authority.  8.2 Moral vs legal modes of existence  Both entries underline a duality: human rights exist as moral claims and as legal instruments, and the relationship between the two matters for legitimacy, enforcement, and critique of sovereignty.  8.3 Universality and pluralism  Human rights claim cross-cultural validity, which generates recurring debates about relativism and ideological bias. The IEP explicitly discusses relativist critiques of universal human rights and notes that these critiques sometimes function as rationalizations for oppression, while also acknowledging real issues about individualism and communal moral systems. A practical framework should therefore include an explicit “universality test”: what, exactly, is being claimed as universal, and how is it justified without cultural domination?  9. Duties, Institutions, and Feasibility 9.1 The duty-bearer question  Rights-based ethics cannot stop at declaring rights; it must specify duty-bearers and duty types. The SEP “Human Rights” entry highlights that human rights duties often require respect, protection, facilitation, and provision, with addressees typically including governments.  9.2 Resource constraints and progressive realization  The “Rights” entry’s Cranston–Nickel exchange is a canonical illustration: the plausibility of welfare rights depends on whether “ought implies can” is applied strictly and whether rights allow progressive implementation and priority-setting. A rights-based framework needs explicit feasibility principles, for example:  Minimum core: some level of protection/provision is non-negotiable.  Progressive realization: full fulfillment can be a structured trajectory.  Non-retrogression: backsliding is presumptively impermissible without strong justification.  9.3 Basic rights and layered duties  Both encyclopedia entries emphasize that the crude negative/positive split obscures how rights work in reality: rights frequently require institutional protection and remedies. Operationally, this pushes rights frameworks toward governance design: what institutions are required for the right not to be merely aspirational?  10. Conflicts, Limits, and the Problem of “Balancing” 10.1 Non-absoluteness and conflict  Rights frameworks must address conflicts between rights (speech vs privacy; liberty vs security; property vs subsistence). The SEP “Human Rights” entry explicitly anticipates disagreement about which rights exist and how to handle them, while preserving a shared “general idea” of human rights.  10.2 Two broad resolution styles  Constraint / trump models (Dworkin-style): rights defeat many goal-arguments, with limited exceptions.  Structured balancing models: rights have weight and can be overridden under stringent conditions (necessity, proportionality, least-restrictive means). Even in balancing approaches, the framework must specify what counts as “rights-violating” versus “rights-limiting,” and what sorts of reasons can justify each.  10.3 Rights inflation and “manifesto rights”  The Encyclopedia.com “Rights Theory” entry warns about “manifesto rights”—asserted rights claims that have not yet been fully warranted by reflective justification and institutional specification. A mature rights-based framework therefore includes an internal audit: does this claim identify a real entitlement with assignable duties and remedies, or is it a moral aspiration mislabeled as a right?  11. Application Domains: Science, Technology, and Biomedicine  Rights talk is especially common where technology creates new powers and vulnerabilities.  11.1 Reproduction, bodily autonomy, and biotechnologies  The “Rights Theory” entry uses reproduction-related disputes (including strong objections to cloning) to illustrate how rights can function as protections against majority moralism—where people seek not only to avoid a practice themselves but to prohibit it for all. A rights-based framework here asks: whose autonomy is at stake, what harms count, and do objections reflect equal respect or “external preferences” that deny equal standing?  11.2 Privacy, surveillance, and data governance  The same entry treats privacy as a paradigmatic rights-issue in technology: surveillance capabilities threaten non-interference and personal security, and rights claims may demand governance mechanisms that restrict collection, mandate transparency, and provide remedies.  11.3 Intellectual property and control over scientific goods  Rights claims can appear as property rights, authorship rights, or entitlements to share in scientific advancement. The framework question is not “is IP good?” but: what entitlements are justified, who bears duties, and how do those entitlements interact with other basic rights (health, access, non-discrimination)?  12. Objections and Persistent Problems 12.1 The “adversarial” character of rights discourse  The Encyclopedia.com “Rights Theory” entry highlights O’Neill’s critique: rights discourse can be adversarial and can obscure duties by focusing on what people “get” rather than what they “ought to do,” and it can appear to promise benefits without confronting costs and duty allocations. Framework implication: pair every rights claim with explicit duty maps and cost-bearing structures to avoid rhetorical overreach.  12.2 Relativism, objectivity, and motivation  The IEP discusses philosophical challenges to the universalist and objectivist bases of human rights and notes that some critics (e.g., Rorty) are skeptical of philosophical foundations while still valuing human rights as a desirable practice, preferring sentimental education over rationalist grounding. Framework implication: distinguish (a) validity questions (are rights true/justified?) from (b) stability/motivation questions (what makes societies actually respect them?).  12.3 Indeterminacy and specification  Abstract rights underdetermine policy. The encyclopedia warning about “manifesto rights” and the SEP emphasis on duties and institutional realization push frameworks toward specification: thresholds, exceptions, remedies, and governance structures.  13. Operational Procedure: A Repeatable “Rights-Based” Method  Use the steps below as a practical template for analysis, design review, or policy ethics.  •	State the rights-claim precisely •	“Right to what?” “against whom?” “in which context?” •	Avoid slogans; express as an entitlement with content. •	Classify the normative relation (Hohfeld audit) •	Is it a claim-right, liberty, power, or immunity? •	Identify correlatives (duty, no-claim, liability, disability). •	Identify right-holders and duty-bearers •	Individuals, groups, children, patients, citizens? •	Duty-bearers: state, institution, professional, corporation, individuals. •	Map duty-types •	Respect / protect / facilitate / provide (or Shue’s forbear / protect / aid). •	Justification checkpoint •	Which grounding is doing the work: interest theory, will theory, equality/concern-and-respect, personhood/agency, or practice-based legitimacy? •	Feasibility and institutional requirements •	What enforcement, courts, oversight, resourcing, or governance is required? •	Note that even “freedom rights” can require costly institutional machinery. •	Conflict scan •	List competing rights and public goods (security, public health, equality, property, speech). •	Decide whether your framework treats relevant rights as trumps/constraints or as weighty but overridable. •	Resolution rule and justification •	If overriding: specify necessity, proportionality/least-restrictive means, and time limits; if trumping: specify the narrow override conditions (if any). •	Remedy and accountability •	What counts as a remedy (cessation, repair, compensation, institutional reform)? •	Who monitors compliance? •	Rights-inflation audit (“manifesto rights” test) •	Are duties assignable and enforceable in principle? •	If not, consider reclassifying as a moral goal rather than a right, or specify what would be needed to make it a warranted claim.  14. Concluding Orientation  A rights-based ethics framework is strongest when it is more than “rights talk.” The most robust versions (i) clarify the type of right at stake, (ii) specify duty-bearers and enforcement pathways, (iii) make their grounding assumptions explicit (interest, will, equality, personhood, practice), and (iv) adopt a transparent method for handling conflicts without collapsing either into absolutism (rights never yield) or into pure trade-offs (rights always negotiable). In contemporary moral philosophy, deontology is one of those kinds of normative theories regarding which choices are morally required, forbidden, or permitted. In other words, deontology falls within the domain of moral theories that guide and assess our choices of what we ought to do (deontic theories), in contrast to those that guide and assess what kind of person we are and should be (aretaic [virtue] theories). And within the domain of moral theories that assess our choices, deontologists—those who subscribe to deontological theories of morality—stand in opposition to consequentialists.  1.
